A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same injectivity and SIPIT research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original collision-search experiments, GPT-2 prompt-inversion accuracy and timing, and appendix analyses of depth, model scale, and sequence length.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds quantized-model evaluations, targeted collision tests, distribution-specific inversion results, and representation-geometry analyses.

M1.justification: SIPIT's sequential reconstruction, local verifier, gradient-guided candidate ranking, and Algorithms 1–3 are retained. Appendix E.1 newly documents gradient clipping, but does not establish a change to the previously used procedure; this is additional implementation disclosure.

E1.justification: v4 retains the Wikipedia, C4, Pile, and Python-code coverage, while adding WebText-based inversion evaluation and English–French translation and arithmetic collision tests using google/smol and ProCreations/SimpleMath. Appendix E.3 also introduces delimiter variations and variable-prefix/fixed-suffix scenarios designed to produce identical next-token predictions.

E2.justification: The corresponding GPT-2 inversion comparison retains HARDPROMPTS and BRUTEFORCE, including the same HARDPROMPTS adaptation. BRUTEFORCE is clarified as the random candidate policy. Newly discussed Thomas et al. (2025) is not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Added protocols include FP4/INT8 weight quantization, 14B/70B model evaluations, inversion of 50 ten-token prompts, and separate groups of 50 hundred-token WebText, Wikipedia, and random prompts. Appendix E adds matched-tokenization controls, approximately 140K delimiter-pair comparisons, 10K fixed-suffix prompts, and geometry measurements using 100 prompts with 1,000 continuations each. The original principal evaluations remain.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained policy, depth, scale, and length analyses, v4 tests quantization robustness, vocabulary-size scaling, and inversion across training-source, unseen, and random sequences. Appendices E.3–E.5 add identical-next-token stress tests, closest-prompt case studies, and analyses relating separation margins to anisotropy and intrinsic dimension.

E5.justification: Appendix E.5 adds Pearson and Spearman correlation estimation across layers. The existing runtime ± reporting is retained without newly specified confidence intervals, significance tests, or increased repeated-run counts. The reproducibility statement drops v1's claim that fixed seeds are supplied.

E6.justification: The original inversion results remain unchanged in v4 Table 5, including SIPIT's 28.01 ± 35.87 seconds and 100% accuracy. New Table 4 reports 100% FP4-model recovery with times of 111.78 ± 46.50 seconds for Mistral-7B-v0.1 and 549.48 ± 265.75 seconds for Llama-3.1-8B. Additional tables report quantized-model separation, targeted collision searches, distribution-specific timings, and geometric correlations. These are added results under new conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: New Appendix F supplies supporting analyticity proofs for sigmoid, SiLU, the error function, GELU, and gated/vector-valued constructions. The central injectivity and training-preservation arguments remain substantively unchanged. Theorem 3.2 brings robustness into the main text, but its margin-based recovery guarantee was already established in v1 Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and central conclusion retain the same contributions: almost-sure injectivity preserved under training and training-free exact reconstruction through SIPIT with a linear verifier-step bound. The expanded evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: Section 3 explicitly distinguishes SIPIT's access to all per-position states from the unresolved problem of efficient inversion using only the final embedding. New discussions interpret quantization, vocabulary scaling, faster random-sequence inversion, and geometric structure. Section 6 also distinguishes inference-time representations from training data encoded in weights, refining the privacy argument.

D1.justification: v4 adds a named SIPIT implementation link and documents gradient clipping at norm 1 and coordinatewise torch.allclose tolerances of 1e-5 relative and 1e-8 absolute. v1 instead claimed an anonymous supplementary repository. The hardware/software description, periodic projection every 50 proposals, and HARDPROMPTS implementation remain.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds Thomas et al. (2025) as a closely related sequential hidden-state inversion method and distinguishes its guarantees. Appendices E.5 and F substantially expand positioning relative to anisotropy, intrinsic dimension, information-bottleneck accounts, universal approximation, and Turing completeness, beyond the earlier related-work discussion.

P1.justification: The main narrative and ordering of the existing theoretical appendices are retained. v4 adds an appendix overview and explanatory roadmaps, standardizes SIPIT terminology, revises selected related-work and reproducibility paragraphs, and updates author affiliations and publication headers. Existing content is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v4 adds Tables 2–4 and 6–12, covering new experiments and the activation survey, plus boxed translation, arithmetic, and code examples. Existing figures are largely retained, but Figures 7–8 move out of the inversion-proof discussion into the experimental appendix, and the main experimental tables and figures are rearranged.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's narrow inversion validation, extending exact recovery beyond GPT-2 to quantized Mistral and Llama models and adding targeted collision and distribution tests. Clearer access limitations, supporting activation proofs, and discussion of the closest prior inverter also improve assessability. Some new interpretations overreach: Table 2 does not support the claim that quantization more than doubles separation in every case, and comparisons between different models do not isolate vocabulary-size effects. These weaknesses limit individual conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial gains in practical evidence and scope clarification.
